All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?

\[
\boxed{\frac15}
\]

The relevant result is the **sharp odd-girth homomorphism-threshold theorem**. Its \(7\)-odd-girth case has the following two parts:

* For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a finite graph \(F_\varepsilon\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that every graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) with
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15+\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \]
  admits a homomorphism to \(F_\varepsilon\).
* For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every finite triangle-free graph \(H\), there is a graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15-\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad G\nrightarrow H.
  \]
  Importantly, this lower-bound statement allows the proposed target \(H\) to contain \(5\)-cycles.

Here, having odd girth at least \(7\) is exactly the condition of containing neither a \(3\)-cycle nor a \(5\)-cycle.

If \(c>1/5\), apply the first part with \(\varepsilon=c-1/5\). The resulting \(F_\varepsilon\) is, in particular, triangle-free, so it can serve as \(H_c\).

Conversely, let \(c<1/5\) and suppose a finite triangle-free target \(H_c\) existed. Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(1/5-\varepsilon>c\). The second part gives a graph satisfying all the hypotheses in the question, with minimum degree greater than \(c|V(G)|\), but with no homomorphism to \(H_c\), a contradiction.

Thus every \(c>1/5\) works and every \(c<1/5\) fails. Whether the endpoint itself works is unnecessary for determining the infimum.

The earlier conclusion \(0\) was incorrect. The key is that allowing pentagons in the target does **not** eliminate the sharp lower-bound obstruction.

For a triangle-free graph \(G\), define \(W_3(G)\) on \(V(G)\) by joining two vertices whenever a walk of length three connects them. Walks may repeat vertices.

### Why this auxiliary graph matters

If \(G\to H\) and \(H\) is triangle-free, then
\[
\chi(W_3(G))\le |V(H)|.
\]
Indeed, color each vertex by its image in \(H\). Equal images at the ends of a three-edge walk would give a closed walk of length three in \(H\), hence a triangle.

Conversely, a \(k\)-coloring \(a\) of \(W_3(G)\) produces a bounded triangle-free target. For each \(v\), set
\[
B(v)=\{a(w):w\in N_G(v)\},
\]
and label \(v\) by \((a(v),B(v))\). Use the finite target whose vertices are pairs
\[
(i,B),\qquad i\in[k],\quad B\subseteq[k]\setminus\{i\},
\]
with adjacency defined by
\[
(i,B)\sim(j,C)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
i\in C,\ j\in B,\ B\cap C=\varnothing.
\]
Every edge of \(G\) is preserved: a color in \(B(u)\cap B(v)\), for \(uv\in E(G)\), would give a three-edge walk with equally colored endpoints. This target is triangle-free, since a third vertex adjacent to both \((i,B)\) and \((j,C)\) would have its first coordinate in \(B\cap C\).

Thus bounded triangle-free targets are equivalent to bounded chromatic number of these auxiliary graphs.

### The sharp extremal input

The substantial input is the sharp odd-girth homomorphism-threshold result, which can be expressed in this auxiliary-graph form:

* For every \(\varepsilon>0\), graphs \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) satisfying
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge\left(\frac15+\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \]
  have \(\chi(W_3(G))\) bounded in terms of \(\varepsilon\).
* For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and integer \(M\), there exists a graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) satisfying
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge\left(\frac15-\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|,
  \qquad \chi(W_3(G))>M.
  \]
  This sharpness statement is what obstructs even targets that are allowed pentagons.

For \(c>1/5\), the first statement and the explicit target above give a single finite triangle-free \(H_c\).

For \(c<1/5\), suppose such an \(H_c\) existed. Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(1/5-\varepsilon>c\), and apply the second statement with \(M=|V(H_c)|\). The resulting \(G\) meets the question’s hypotheses but cannot map to \(H_c\), by the auxiliary chromatic-number bound.

Hence every \(c>1/5\) works and every \(c<1/5\) fails, proving the stated infimum. The endpoint itself need not be decided.
